title: Intro to Subspace Lattice
youtubeTitle: What Is Subspace Lattice? — Beginner’s Guide (How to Play & How to Win)
description: A friendly first look at Subspace Lattice: what the game is, why its pure logic is so engaging, how a match feels, and the three ways to win. Play free at lattice.iwgf.org.

scenes.headline: What is Subspace Lattice?
scenes.subhead: A two-player fleet duel — chess tactics, a growing Sensor Net, and one job: take their Command Hub.
scenes.voiceover: Welcome to Sector 11, a dead zone shattered by a collapsed stellar core. Space isn't empty here; it's unclaimed. Two fleets drop in, and nothing out there is yours until you claim it. This is Subspace Lattice — a two-player strategy game where you command a signal fleet. You don't just sail through a sector; you weave the Subspace Lattice through it, thread by thread, and make it yours.

scenes.headline: Your mission in one breath
bullets: You are a captain with a small fleet
Your Command Hub is your flagship and power anchor
You hunt theirs — while your Sensor Net grows
scenes.voiceover: Commanding a strike fleet in this dead space requires a singular anchor. Your Command Hub is your flagship and power anchor. Every tactical signal flows outward from it, turning linked ships into a lethal, expanding web. Hiding behind static shields won't save anyone out here. You are hunting the opposing flagship, choking off their power, and weaving a Sensor Net that turns endless stalling into a guaranteed lockout.

This is the board: an 11 by 11 grid. The center cell is a Gravity Well, which acts as an Anomalous Core singularity. Gravity Wells block pieces; they may not occupy or make a path through them. Blue glow is White’s Sensor Net. Red is Black’s. That glow is not decoration — it is where your Beams can move, and where enemy ships get Target Locked.

scenes.headline: Your fleet — four kinds of ship
bullets: Command Hub — your flagship and power anchor
Escorts — subspace repeaters that carry the network outward
Infiltrators — folding-drive phase runner strike craft that jump independent of any signal
Beams — dreadnoughts that can only fire while riding an active net
scenes.voiceover: The pieces are a signal fleet. The Command Hub is your flagship and power anchor. Escorts are subspace repeaters that carry the network outward. Infiltrators are folding-drive phase runners that jump independent of any signal. Beams are dreadnoughts that can only fire while riding an active net. The academy boards in this series leave Infiltrators out so the Hub hunt stays readable. Lose your Hub and the battle ends.

The Sensor Net is the heart of the game. Your Hub always broadcasts a wide field. Escorts radiate a radius only if linked to the Command Hub by a distance of at most two squares. Push Escorts forward and the glow grows. Break the chain and a distant Escort goes dark.

scenes.headline: Target Lock — punish overreach
bullets: A piece is Target Locked if its current coordinate lies in the opponent's Sensor Net
While Target Locked, the piece loses special movement and may only move one orthogonal step
A locked Beam can’t do Beam things
scenes.voiceover: Cross into the enemy's glow and their net has you now, Target Locked to a single crawling step. A piece is Target Locked if its current coordinate lies in the opponent's Sensor Net. While Target Locked, the piece loses special movement and may only move one orthogonal step. That is how the net punishes overextension.

scenes.headline: Why it’s fun
bullets: Tactics you can see built on flawless logic
A living map of coverage that shifts every move
Win by precision capture or by late-game coverage pressure
scenes.voiceover: Why people stick with it: every turn asks a sharp question without needing a thousand-page opening book. This is a game built on flawless mathematical logic rather than mechanical chance, rewarding tight, perfect-information strategy over lucky breaks. Captures feel decisive. Coverage builds a second story for games that dig in.

scenes.headline: How to play — the first ten minutes
bullets: Link Escorts so the net reaches midboard
Slide Beams into files that will matter later
Refuse the hang; Hub safety always comes first
Look for their Hub sitting on an open Beam file
scenes.voiceover: How to play, simply. Early on: advance central Escorts, keep them linked, and grow the glow toward the middle. Pre-position Beams inside your net so they have lanes when the fight opens. Midgame: Target Locks and trades — but refuse the hang; Hub safety always comes first. If their Hub shares a file with your Beam and the path is clear, that is often the whole game.

How you win, number one — Surgical Strike. Surgical Strike is the primary tactical resolution. Capture the enemy Command Hub to win immediately. Most games are playing toward this. One careless step, one prepared Beam or Escort, and the battle ends.

How you win, number two — Sector Integration. The sector clock is disarmed before 100 completed plies. After activation, if your Sensor Net covers at least 45% of all non-Gravity-Well coordinates, you win. The seams where both nets bleed together are Contested Space and answer to neither side, so a defender can stall your clock by pushing into your glow. It ensures turtling forever doesn’t work.

scenes.headline: Three ways to win
bullets: Surgical Strike — capture their Command Hub
Sector Integration — hold 45% coverage after the clock arms
Lockout — the opponent has no legal move
scenes.voiceover: So, the three wins are Surgical Strike, Sector Integration, and no legal moves. Surgical Strike decides most games. Sector Integration decides the long sieges. And third, rare but real: if your opponent has no legal move at all, they lose. Play for the first, respect the second, and remember the third exists.

scenes.headline: How a game feels
bullets: Opening — link up, contest the middle
Midgame — locks, trades, Hub hunts
Late — strike if you can; otherwise the clock decides
scenes.voiceover: A typical match: open by linking and contesting the midboard. Midgame is net fights and Target Locks, probing for a Hub mistake. Late game, either you convert Surgical Strike, or the clock arms and coverage starts to decide it. Good play looks like fleet tactics on a shifting Sensor Net—not a race to paint cells.
